sections.sectionSummaryBrief: This section discusses the Rebbe's 1927 talk on the verse "Yihi Hashem Elokeinu imanu," explaining how it combines both a request and a promise.

translations.translation: "May Hashem our G-d be with us as He was with our fathers; may He not forsake us nor abandon us."
And known is the talk of the Baal HaGeulah, who said on 3 Tammuz 5687,
"We ask of Hashem Yisbarach,
'May Hashem our G-d be with us as He was with our fathers; may He not forsake us nor abandon us,'
Hashem Yisbarach should be with us,
and He will be with us as He was with our fathers."
And it needs to be understood: a request and a promise are different matters
(and seemingly even opposites),
and nevertheless he says, "We ask of Hashem Yisbarach... should be with us and will be with us,"
that the request is
(not only "should be with us" but also)
"will be with us."
And although the word "Yihi" is a term of request and also a term of promise,
these are seemingly different interpretations
(matters)
[different],
and in the talk he includes both matters together.

sections.sectionSummaryBrief: This section explains the paradox that the request and promise apply even though we are not equal to the forefathers, citing a Midrash about hiring bad workers, and questions how the Rebbe could say this while himself being a paradigm of self-sacrifice.

translations.translation: And he continues in the talk,
"That this 'May Hashem our G-d be with us as He was with our fathers'
('Yihi' in the language of request and also in the language of promise)
is despite the fact that we are indeed not equal to our fathers."
And it can be said,
that the source for this explanation is what is brought in the Midrash:
"And Shlomo says before the Holy One, blessed be He: A king who hires workers and they do their work well and he pays them their wages—what praise is there for the king?
And when is he praised? When he hires bad workers
who do not do their work, and he pays them their wages—this is a great goodness. And so it says, 'May Hashem our G-d be with us as He was with our fathers.'"
And he explains in the talk that this inability to be compared to our fathers is because our fathers were people of actual self-sacrifice (mesirus nefesh) for Torah and mitzvos.
And it needs to be understood:
After all, the delivery of this talk was in connection with his journey into exile in Kostrama,
that the exile
(and before that the imprisonment)
was because of his actual self-sacrifice for Torah and mitzvos
[and even more so,
that even the very utterance of this talk was actual self-sacrifice],
and nevertheless he says that we are not comparable to our fathers, who were people of self-sacrifice.
